requests.question: Briefly explain the five-minute oxytocin finding, its possible relevance to felt connection, and whether the four 528 Hz RCTs all used blinding. Include the trial-size range.

response.answer:
**Five-minute finding:** Oxytocin almost doubled within five minutes of listening to 528 Hz music. The increase with 440 Hz music was not statistically significant. In Akimoto’s 2018 crossover study of **nine healthy adults**, mean salivary oxytocin rose from **37.57 to 73.58 pg/mL** (p < 0.038). This was a before–after change within the 528 Hz condition—not a doubling relative to the 440 Hz condition. The small sample and short-term measurements limit conclusions. [S1]

**Possible relevance to felt connection:** Oxytocin’s involvement in social bonding makes increased felt connection a research hypothesis. The saliva finding does **not** establish that listeners felt more connected or demonstrate a causal brain pathway. [S2]

**Trial sizes and blinding:** The four explicitly 528 Hz RCTs ranged from **48–162 participants total**, with **24–54 participants in the 528 Hz groups**. The broader research family includes tones, tuned music and chanting. [S2]

Blinding was **not established across all four**:
- **Heti, Bhoot and Bozok:** blinding was not clearly reported. That is a reporting limitation, not proof that no blinding occurred. [S3][S4][S5]
- **Ravikumar:** blood-pressure assessors and cortisol laboratory personnel were blinded. Participant blinding was also reported, but its implementation is unclear because the intervention was delivered in person and the control remotely. [S6]

Random allocation and a comparison condition establish an RCT; blinding is a separate design feature.

sources.label: S3
sources.title: 528Hz: The Sound Of Tranquillity And Its Effect On Anxiety
sources.text: A three-minute exposure described as a pure 528 Hz tone was compared with neutral reading. Mean state-anxiety scores fell by 4.63 points in the sound group and 0.83 in controls; the reported time-by-group interaction was p = .036.

sources.label: S4
sources.title: Effect of OM Chanting of 528Hz Frequency on Heart Rate Variability, Psychological Wellbeing, and Quality of Sleep in Patients of Hypertension: A Randomised Controlled Trial
sources.authors: Bhoot A, Chowdhury AB, Shah H, Vaishnav B.
sources.text: Fifteen minutes of daily listening to 528 Hz OM chanting plus standard care produced promising blood-pressure and perceived-stress results against standard care. Pulse and systolic-pressure time-by-group interactions were significant; SDNN and RMSSD interactions were not. Between-group sleep and total wellbeing differences were not significant.

sources.label: S5
sources.title: Acute Music-Frequency Exposure Modulates Salivary Stress and Neurotrophic Markers in Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.authors: Bozok ÜG, Böyük Özcan G, Bayraktar B, Özen D.
sources.text: After 20 minutes of 528 Hz-labelled instrumental music, salivary CREB was higher and GRP78 lower than in the no-music group. Stroop performance did not differ. Table 1 gives 528 Hz and control the same BDNF significance label, despite the more positive abstract.

sources.label: S6
sources.title: Effects of a Sound-Based Meditative Intervention on Anxiety, Depression, Salivary Cortisol Levels, and Blood Pressure: A Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.text: Daily sound meditation incorporating recorded 528 Hz audio and acoustic instruments outperformed remotely delivered music on anxiety, depression, salivary cortisol and blood pressure. Adjusted differences included HADS anxiety −2.55 points (95% CI −3.62 to −1.48) and cortisol −2.54 nmol/L (−2.95 to −2.13).
